new way to make hydrogen fuel
[URL=http://www.newscientist.com/article/mg19726470.600-a-new-way-to-make-hydrogen-fuel.html?DCMP=OTC-rss&nsref=&utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=scitech-2010_10_22][IMG]http://i.cdn.turner.com/cnn/.element/img/logos/newscorp.png[/IMG][/URL]
A new way to produce the clean-burning gas could help solve one of its biggest problems: how do you store it?
By David Shukman, New Scientist 21 October 2009
The world's energy needs are growing fast and fossil fuels such as oil will run out in a few decades at current rates.
But there is another source that can be used instead - hydrogen produced from water using renewable electricity or nuclear power. The problem with this approach has been finding an efficient method for storing large amounts of hydrogen safely until needed.
Now researchers have come up with what they say may well prove to be "the holy grail" solution by developing a material capable of absorbing huge quantities of hydrogen without losing any when released again later on demand (New Journal Of Chemistry, doi.org/bq).
Hydrogen storage materials fall into two categories – those which absorb lots but release little back; these tend not to hold much more than about half their weight in H2 molecules per gramme of solid matter. Then there are ones like palladium metal alloys where most absorbed goes straight back out again once pressure drops off after use.
This latest discovery comes close to solving both issues because it absorbs around three times its own mass while releasing almost all of it easily enough under normal conditions.
It also does so over temperatures ranging between minus 100 degrees Celsius (-148 °F) right through to plus 300°C (+572°F), making it suitable even for cold climates.
"We've found something really special," says lead researcher Michael Asta of Northwestern University in Evanston Illinois who presented his findings last week during the American Chemical Society meeting here in San Francisco.
He believes he now knows why some metals form strong bonds with hydrogen atoms, allowing them to take up vast volumes before letting go readily afterwards.
"The key seems to lie in atomic structure rather than chemical bonding", explains astrophysicists John Kasting of Pennsylvania State University in University Park whose group first identified the phenomenon several years ago.
Kasting points out that many elements including carbon, silicon and germanium exist naturally bonded together inside rocks called silicates. These minerals contain oxygen too along with other light-weight gases such as nitrogen and helium.
When heated strongly above four thousand kelvins (~4000° C / ~7300° F ), however, these compounds break down leaving behind pure elemental forms of each element present within.
In particular, heating causes certain types of silica-based rock known collectively as olivine to split apart producing magnesium oxide mixed with iron oxides among others.
These reactions occur deep underground beneath Earth’s surface long before molten magma rises upwards towards volcanoes erupting onto land surfaces near sea level.
As soon'this happens though, atmospheric pressures drop sharply causing hot lava flows containing dissolved gasses to cool rapidly leading eventually to crystallisation forming crystals rich in heavy metallic ions surrounded by lighter non-metallic cations.
Such structures resemble closely related arrangements seen elsewhere throughout nature suggesting common origins dating perhaps billions of years earlier still.
Indeed scientists believe our planet itself formed via similar processes involving collisions amongst smaller bodies orbiting nearby stars millions upon trillions kilometres away across interstellar space.
So far no-one else appears aware yet either of exactly how these exotic substances work nor precisely just what role if indeed any might play ultimately determining future fates awaiting humanity beyond mere survival alone…

A new way to produce the clean-burning gas could help solve one of its biggest problems: how do you store it?
By David Shukman, New Scientist 21 October 2009
The world's energy needs are growing fast and fossil fuels such as oil will run out in a few decades at current rates.
But there is another source that can be used instead - hydrogen produced from water using renewable electricity or nuclear power. The problem with this approach has been finding an efficient method for storing large amounts of hydrogen safely until needed.
Now researchers have come up with what they say may well prove to be "the holy grail" solution by developing a material capable of absorbing huge quantities of hydrogen without losing any when released again later on demand (New Journal Of Chemistry, doi.org/bq).
Hydrogen storage materials fall into two categories – those which absorb lots but release little back; these tend not to hold much more than about half their weight in H2 molecules per gramme of solid matter. Then there are ones like palladium metal alloys where most absorbed goes straight back out again once pressure drops off after use.
This latest discovery comes close to solving both issues because it absorbs around three times its own mass while releasing almost all of it easily enough under normal conditions.
It also does so over temperatures ranging between minus 100 degrees Celsius (-148 °F) right through to plus 300°C (+572°F), making it suitable even for cold climates.
"We've found something really special," says lead researcher Michael Asta of Northwestern University in Evanston Illinois who presented his findings last week during the American Chemical Society meeting here in San Francisco.
He believes he now knows why some metals form strong bonds with hydrogen atoms, allowing them to take up vast volumes before letting go readily afterwards.
"The key seems to lie in atomic structure rather than chemical bonding", explains astrophysicists John Kasting of Pennsylvania State University in University Park whose group first identified the phenomenon several years ago.
Kasting points out that many elements including carbon, silicon and germanium exist naturally bonded together inside rocks called silicates. These minerals contain oxygen too along with other light-weight gases such as nitrogen and helium.
When heated strongly above four thousand kelvins (~4000° C / ~7300° F ), however, these compounds break down leaving behind pure elemental forms of each element present within.
In particular, heating causes certain types of silica-based rock known collectively as olivine to split apart producing magnesium oxide mixed with iron oxides among others.
These reactions occur deep underground beneath Earth’s surface long before molten magma rises upwards towards volcanoes erupting onto land surfaces near sea level.
As soon'this happens though, atmospheric pressures drop sharply causing hot lava flows containing dissolved gasses to cool rapidly leading eventually to crystallisation forming crystals rich in heavy metallic ions surrounded by lighter non-metallic cations.
Such structures resemble closely related arrangements seen elsewhere throughout nature suggesting common origins dating perhaps billions of years earlier still.
Indeed scientists believe our planet itself formed via similar processes involving collisions amongst smaller bodies orbiting nearby stars millions upon trillions kilometres away across interstellar space.
So far no-one else appears aware yet either of exactly how these exotic substances work nor precisely just what role if indeed any might play ultimately determining future fates awaiting humanity beyond mere survival alone…

[URL=http://www.newscientist.com/article/mg19726470.600-a-new-way-to-make-hydrogen-fuel.html?DCMP=OTC-rss&nsref=&utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=scitech-2010_10_22][IMG]http://i.cdn.turner.com/cnn/.element/img/logos/newscorp.png[/IMG][/URL]
A new way to produce the clean-burning gas could help solve one of its biggest problems: how do you store it?
By David Shukman, New Scientist 21 October 2009
The world's energy needs are growing fast and fossil fuels such as oil will run out in a few decades at current rates.
But there is another source that can be used instead - hydrogen produced from water using renewable electricity or nuclear power. The problem with this approach has been finding an efficient method for storing large amounts of hydrogen safely until needed.
Now researchers have come up with what they say may well prove to be "the holy grail" solution by developing a material capable of absorbing huge quantities of hydrogen without losing any when released again later on demand (New Journal Of Chemistry, doi.org/bq).
Hydrogen storage materials fall into two categories – those which absorb lots but release little back; these tend not to hold much more than about half their weight in H2 molecules per gramme of solid matter. Then there are ones like palladium metal alloys where most absorbed goes straight back out again once pressure drops off after use.
This latest discovery comes close to solving both issues because it absorbs around three times its own mass while releasing almost all of it easily enough under normal conditions.
It also does so over temperatures ranging between minus 100 degrees Celsius (-148 °F) right through to plus 300°C (+572°F), making it suitable even for cold climates.
"We've found something really special," says lead researcher Michael Asta of Northwestern University in Evanston Illinois who presented his findings last week during the American Chemical Society meeting here in San Francisco.
He believes he now knows why some metals form strong bonds with hydrogen atoms, allowing them to take up vast volumes before letting go readily afterwards.
"The key seems to lie in atomic structure rather than chemical bonding", explains astrophysicists John Kasting of Pennsylvania State University in University Park whose group first identified the phenomenon several years ago.
Kasting points out that many elements including carbon, silicon and germanium exist naturally bonded together inside rocks called silicates. These minerals contain oxygen too along with other light-weight gases such as nitrogen and helium.
When heated strongly above four thousand kelvins (~4000° C / ~7300° F ), however, these compounds break down leaving behind pure elemental forms of each element present within.
In particular, heating causes certain types of silica-based rock known collectively as olivine to split apart producing magnesium oxide mixed with iron oxides among others.
These reactions occur deep underground beneath Earth’s surface long before molten magma rises upwards towards volcanoes erupting onto land surfaces near sea level.
As soon'this happens though, atmospheric pressures drop sharply causing hot lava flows containing dissolved gasses to cool rapidly leading eventually to crystallisation forming crystals rich in heavy metallic ions surrounded by lighter non-metallic cations.
Such structures resemble closely related arrangements seen elsewhere throughout nature suggesting common origins dating perhaps billions of years earlier still.
Indeed scientists believe our planet itself formed via similar processes involving collisions amongst smaller bodies orbiting nearby stars millions upon trillions kilometres away across interstellar space.
So far no-one else appears aware yet either of exactly how these exotic substances work nor precisely just what role if indeed any might play ultimately determining future fates awaiting humanity beyond mere survival alone…

[URL=http://www.newscientist.com/article/mg19726470.600-a-new-way-to-make-hydrogen-fuel.html?DCMP=OTC-rss&nsref=&utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=scitech-2010_10_22][IMG]http://i.cdn.turner.com/cnn/.element/img/logos/newscorp.png[/IMG][/URL]
A new way to produce the clean-burning gas could help solve one of its biggest problems: how do you store it?
By David Shukman, New Scientist 21 October 2009
The world's energy needs are growing fast and fossil fuels such as oil will run out in a few decades at current rates.
But there is another source that can be used instead - hydrogen produced from water using renewable electricity or nuclear power. The problem with this approach has been finding an efficient method for storing large amounts of hydrogen safely until needed.
Now researchers have come up with what they say may well prove to be "the holy grail" solution by developing a material capable of absorbing huge quantities of hydrogen without losing any when released again later on demand (New Journal Of Chemistry, doi.org/bq).
Hydrogen storage materials fall into two categories – those which absorb lots but release little back; these tend not to hold much more than about half their weight in H2 molecules per gramme of solid matter. Then there are ones like palladium metal alloys where most absorbed goes straight back out again once pressure drops off after use.
This latest discovery comes close to solving both issues because it absorbs around three times its own mass while releasing almost all of it easily enough under normal conditions.
It also does so over temperatures ranging between minus 100 degrees Celsius (-148 °F) right through to plus 300°C (+572°F), making it suitable even for cold climates.
"We've found something really special," says lead researcher Michael Asta of Northwestern University in Evanston Illinois who presented his findings last week during the American Chemical Society meeting here in San Francisco.
He believes he now knows why some metals form strong bonds with hydrogen atoms, allowing them to take up vast volumes before letting go readily afterwards.
"The key seems to lie in atomic structure rather than chemical bonding", explains astrophysicists John Kasting of Pennsylvania State University in University Park whose group first identified the phenomenon several years ago.
Kasting points out that many elements including carbon, silicon and germanium exist naturally bonded together inside rocks called silicates. These minerals contain oxygen too along with other light-weight gases such as nitrogen and helium.
When heated strongly above four thousand kelvins (~4000° C / ~7300° F ), however, these compounds break down leaving behind pure elemental forms of each element present within.
In particular, heating causes certain types of silica-based rock known collectively as olivine to split apart producing magnesium oxide mixed with iron oxides among others.
These reactions occur deep underground beneath Earth’s surface long before molten magma rises upwards towards volcanoes erupting onto land surfaces near sea level.
As soon'this happens though, atmospheric pressures drop sharply causing hot lava flows containing dissolved gasses to cool rapidly leading eventually to crystallisation forming crystals rich in heavy metallic ions surrounded by lighter non-metallic cations.
Such structures resemble closely related arrangements seen elsewhere throughout nature suggesting common origins dating perhaps billions of years earlier still.
Indeed scientists believe our planet itself formed via similar processes involving collisions amongst smaller bodies orbiting nearby stars millions upon trillions kilometres away across interstellar space.
So far no-one else appears aware yet either of exactly how these exotic substances work nor precisely just what role if indeed any might play ultimately determining future fates awaiting humanity beyond mere survival alone…

A new way to produce the clean-burning gas could help solve one of its biggest problems: how do you store it?
By David Shukman, New Scientist 21 October 2009
The world's energy needs are growing fast and fossil fuels such as oil will run out in a few decades at current rates.
But there is another source that can be used instead - hydrogen produced from water using renewable electricity or nuclear power. The problem with this approach has been finding an efficient method for storing large amounts of hydrogen safely until needed.
Now researchers have come up with what they say may well prove to be "the holy grail" solution by developing a material capable of absorbing huge quantities of hydrogen without losing any when released again later on demand (New Journal Of Chemistry, doi.org/bq).
Hydrogen storage materials fall into two categories – those which absorb lots but release little back; these tend not to hold much more than about half their weight in H2 molecules per gramme of solid matter. Then there are ones like palladium metal alloys where most absorbed goes straight back out again once pressure drops off after use.
This latest discovery comes close to solving both issues because it absorbs around three times its own mass while releasing almost all of it easily enough under normal conditions.
It also does so over temperatures ranging between minus 100 degrees Celsius (-148 °F) right through to plus 300°C (+572°F), making it suitable even for cold climates.
"We've found something really special," says lead researcher Michael Asta of Northwestern University in Evanston Illinois who presented his findings last week during the American Chemical Society meeting here in San Francisco.
He believes he now knows why some metals form strong bonds with hydrogen atoms, allowing them to take up vast volumes before letting go readily afterwards.
"The key seems to lie in atomic structure rather than chemical bonding", explains astrophysicists John Kasting of Pennsylvania State University in University Park whose group first identified the phenomenon several years ago.
Kasting points out that many elements including carbon, silicon and germanium exist naturally bonded together inside rocks called silicates. These minerals contain oxygen too along with other light-weight gases such as nitrogen and helium.
When heated strongly above four thousand kelvins (~4000° C / ~7300° F ), however, these compounds break down leaving behind pure elemental forms of each element present within.
In particular, heating causes certain types of silica-based rock known collectively as olivine to split apart producing magnesium oxide mixed with iron oxides among others.
These reactions occur deep underground beneath Earth’s surface long before molten magma rises upwards towards volcanoes erupting onto land surfaces near sea level.
As soon'this happens though, atmospheric pressures drop sharply causing hot lava flows containing dissolved gasses to cool rapidly leading eventually to crystallisation forming crystals rich in heavy metallic ions surrounded by lighter non-metallic cations.
Such structures resemble closely related arrangements seen elsewhere throughout nature suggesting common origins dating perhaps billions of years earlier still.
Indeed scientists believe our planet itself formed via similar processes involving collisions amongst smaller bodies orbiting nearby stars millions upon trillions kilometres away across interstellar space.
So far no-one else appears aware yet either of exactly how these exotic substances work nor precisely just what role if indeed any might play ultimately determining future fates awaiting humanity beyond mere survival alone…

A new way to produce the clean-burning gas could help solve one of its biggest problems: how do you store it?
By David Shukman, New Scientist 21 October 2009
The world's energy needs are growing fast and fossil fuels such as oil will run out in a few decades at current rates.
But there is another source that can be used instead - hydrogen produced from water using renewable electricity or nuclear power. The problem with this approach has been finding an efficient method for storing large amounts of hydrogen safely until needed.
Now researchers have come up with what they say may well prove to be "the holy grail" solution by developing a material capable of absorbing huge quantities of hydrogen without losing any when released again later on demand (New Journal Of Chemistry, doi.org/bq).
Hydrogen storage materials fall into two categories – those which absorb lots but release little back; these tend not to hold much more than about half their weight in H2 molecules per gramme of solid matter. Then there are ones like palladium metal alloys where most absorbed goes straight back out again once pressure drops off after use.
This latest discovery comes close to solving both issues because it absorbs around three times its own mass while releasing almost all of it easily enough under normal conditions.
It also does so over temperatures ranging between minus 100 degrees Celsius (-148 °F) right through to plus 300°C (+572°F), making it suitable even for cold climates.
"We've found something really special," says lead researcher Michael Asta of Northwestern University in Evanston Illinois who presented his findings last week during the American Chemical Society meeting here in San Francisco.
He believes he now knows why some metals form strong bonds with hydrogen atoms, allowing them to take up vast volumes before letting go readily afterwards.
"The key seems to lie in atomic structure rather than chemical bonding", explains astrophysicists John Kasting of Pennsylvania State University in University Park whose group first identified the phenomenon several years ago.
Kasting points out that many elements including carbon, silicon and germanium exist naturally bonded together inside rocks called silicates. These minerals contain oxygen too along with other light-weight gases such as nitrogen and helium.
When heated strongly above four thousand kelvins (~4000° C / ~7300° F ), however, these compounds break down leaving behind pure elemental forms of each element present within.
In particular, heating causes certain types of silica-based rock known collectively as olivine to split apart producing magnesium oxide mixed with iron oxides among others.
These reactions occur deep underground beneath Earth’s surface long before molten magma rises upwards towards volcanoes erupting onto land surfaces near sea level.
As soon'this happens though, atmospheric pressures drop sharply causing hot lava flows containing dissolved gasses to cool rapidly leading eventually to crystallisation forming crystals rich in heavy metallic ions surrounded by lighter non-metallic cations.
Such structures resemble closely related arrangements seen elsewhere throughout nature suggesting common origins dating perhaps billions of years earlier still.
Indeed scientists believe our planet itself formed via similar processes involving collisions amongst smaller bodies orbiting nearby stars millions upon trillions kilometres away across interstellar space.
So far no-one else appears aware yet either of exactly how these exotic substances work nor precisely just what role if indeed any might play ultimately determining future fates awaiting humanity beyond mere survival alone…

[ANS] A Very Retro Question - by J. R. Minkel, Scientific American (2007-10)
A few years ago I was in a bar with some friends when the topic of quantum mechanics came up.
One friend asked me what it would take to prove that there is no such thing as "quantum reality." In other words: What experiment could you do today or tomorrow--or even next week!--that might convince someone who believes in quantum theory and its predictions about how we should behave?
I didn't have an answer then; now I think my response probably wouldn't be much different than before. But this got me thinking again recently while reading through old issues of Physics Today . One article from 1969 caught my eye:
"Quantization," wrote physicist John Wheeler at Princeton University back then,
"is not yet complete.... The problem remains unsolved...of finding out whether nature has any preferred states."
Wheeler's comment reminded me of another one he made more than two decades later during his acceptance speech for the Nobel Prize in physics :
"I am still waiting for Godot!"
The reference here isn't just to Samuel Beckett 's play Waiting For Godot , but also to Eugene Wigner 's famous paper on the role of probability in science .
In fact, both quotes are related because they're part of a larger discussion between physicists Richard Feynman and Freeman Dyson over why certain experiments haven't been done despite their obvious importance.
Feynman had argued against doing them based partly upon philosophical grounds. He believed that if scientists were able to perform these tests, people like Einstein --who thought that all physical laws must follow logically from basic principles--would reject those results without hesitation. And since most theoretical work proceeds under assumptions similar to Einstein's own, experimentalists shouldn’t bother trying until after theorists come around first.
Dyson disagreed strongly with this view, arguing instead that only rigorous testing can lead us closer towards understanding our universe’s true structure. As long as theories remain untested, said Dyson, “we will never know which ones deserve respect.”
So where does that leave things? Well, according to Wheeler himself--
“Godot” means nothing special except that it refers to something important happening sometime soon...
And although many believe that time travel may someday become possible, nobody knows exactly how far away that day really lies!

Two Little Words That Could Save Your Life – And Maybe Even Our Planet!
By Dr. Michael Egnor on December 4th, 2018 at 11:00 am | Filed in Health & Wellness |
The two most important and least understood concepts of modern medicine are “cause” and “effect.” They’re so simple they seem obvious.
But when you think about it for a minute or two, their meaning becomes clear:
Cause is what happens first; effect comes later.
If I cut my finger with an Xacto knife, then bleed from the wound, cause was cutting myself with the blade — which happened before bleeding occurred as its consequence.
Effect means something follows another thing. Cause precedes effects because causes happen earlier than consequences do.
In science we use these terms to describe how things work together. If A occurs after B does, scientists say there’s evidence that one caused the other.
For example, if someone gets sick right away after eating contaminated food, doctors will conclude that bacteria in the tainted meal made them ill.
Or consider this scenario: You get into your car late Friday night and drive home through heavy rainstorms all weekend long until Monday morning arrives bright and sunny again. What did those storms have anything to do with clearing up?
Well, no direct connection exists between weather conditions over three days ago and today being dry outside. But since Sunday afternoon brought sunshine while Saturday evening had been rainy, many people would assume some sort of causal relationship existed here too.
This idea isn’t just limited to natural phenomena either—human actions often follow predictable patterns based upon past events leading us towards certain outcomes without any conscious effort involved whatsoever! For instance,
A person who has never experienced success may feel discouraged even though he hasn’t tried very hard yet… but once failure strikes repeatedly enough times eventually leads him down such dark paths where giving up seems like his only option left…

A new way to produce the clean-burning gas could help solve one of its biggest problems: how do you store it?
By David Shukman, New Scientist 21 October 2009
The world's energy needs are growing fast and fossil fuels such as oil will run out in a few decades at current rates.
But there is another source that can be used instead - hydrogen produced from water using renewable electricity or nuclear power. The problem with this approach has been finding an efficient method for storing large amounts of hydrogen safely until needed.
Now researchers have come up with what they say may well prove to be "the holy grail" solution by developing a material capable of absorbing huge quantities of hydrogen without losing any when released again later on demand (New Journal Of Chemistry, doi.org/bq).
Hydrogen storage materials fall into two categories – those which absorb lots but release little back; these tend not to hold much more than about half their weight in H2 molecules per gramme of solid matter. Then there are ones like palladium metal alloys where most absorbed goes straight back out again once pressure drops off after use.
This latest discovery comes close to solving both issues because it absorbs around three times its own mass while releasing almost all of it easily enough under normal conditions.
It also does so over temperatures ranging between minus 100 degrees Celsius (-148 °F) right through to plus 300°C (+572°F), making it suitable even for cold climates.
"We've found something really special," says lead researcher Michael Asta of Northwestern University in Evanston Illinois who presented his findings last week during the American Chemical Society meeting here in San Francisco.
He believes he now knows why some metals form strong bonds with hydrogen atoms, allowing them to take up vast volumes before letting go readily afterwards.
"The key seems to lie in atomic structure rather than chemical bonding", explains astrophysicists John Kasting of Pennsylvania State University in University Park whose group first identified the phenomenon several years ago.
Kasting points out that many elements including carbon, silicon and germanium exist naturally bonded together inside rocks called silicates. These minerals contain oxygen too along with other light-weight gases such as nitrogen and helium.
When heated strongly above four thousand kelvins (~4000° C / ~7300° F ), however, these compounds break down leaving behind pure elemental forms of each element present within.
In particular, heating causes certain types of silica-based rock known collectively as olivine to split apart producing magnesium oxide mixed with iron oxides among others.
These reactions occur deep underground beneath Earth’s surface long before molten magma rises upwards towards volcanoes erupting onto land surfaces near sea level.
As soon'this happens though, atmospheric pressures drop sharply causing hot lava flows containing dissolved gasses to cool rapidly leading eventually to crystallisation forming crystals rich in heavy metallic ions surrounded by lighter non-metallic cations.
Such structures resemble closely related arrangements seen elsewhere throughout nature suggesting common origins dating perhaps billions of years earlier still.
Indeed scientists believe our planet itself formed via similar processes involving collisions amongst smaller bodies orbiting nearby stars millions upon trillions kilometres away across interstellar space.
So far no-one else appears aware yet either of exactly how these exotic substances work nor precisely just what role if indeed any might play ultimately determining future fates awaiting humanity beyond mere survival alone…

A new way to produce the clean-burning gas could help solve one of its biggest problems: how do you store it?
By David Shukman, New Scientist 21 October 2009
The world's energy needs are growing fast and fossil fuels such as oil will run out in a few decades at current rates.
But there is another source that can be used instead - hydrogen produced from water using renewable electricity or nuclear power. The problem with this approach has been finding an efficient method for storing large amounts of hydrogen safely until needed.
Now researchers have come up with what they say may well prove to be "the holy grail" solution by developing a material capable of absorbing huge quantities of hydrogen without losing any when released again later on demand (New Journal Of Chemistry, doi.org/bq).
Hydrogen storage materials fall into two categories – those which absorb lots but release little back; these tend not to hold much more than about half their weight in H2 molecules per gramme of solid matter. Then there are ones like palladium metal alloys where most absorbed goes straight back out again once pressure drops off after use.
This latest discovery comes close to solving both issues because it absorbs around three times its own mass while releasing almost all of it easily enough under normal conditions.
It also does so over temperatures ranging between minus 100 degrees Celsius (-148 °F) right through to plus 300°C (+572°F), making it suitable even for cold climates.
"We've found something really special," says lead researcher Michael Asta of Northwestern University in Evanston Illinois who presented his findings last week during the American Chemical Society meeting here in San Francisco.
He believes he now knows why some metals form strong bonds with hydrogen atoms, allowing them to take up vast volumes before letting go readily afterwards.
"The key seems to lie in atomic structure rather than chemical bonding", explains astrophysicists John Kasting of Pennsylvania State University in University Park whose group first identified the phenomenon several years ago.
Kasting points out that many elements including carbon, silicon and germanium exist naturally bonded together inside rocks called silicates. These minerals contain oxygen too along with other light-weight gases such as nitrogen and helium.
When heated strongly above four thousand kelvins (~4000° C / ~7300° F ), however, these compounds break down leaving behind pure elemental forms of each element present within.
In particular, heating causes certain types of silica-based rock known collectively as olivine to split apart producing magnesium oxide mixed with iron oxides among others.
These reactions occur deep underground beneath Earth’s surface long before molten magma rises upwards towards volcanoes erupting onto land surfaces near sea level.
As soon'this happens though, atmospheric pressures drop sharply causing hot lava flows containing dissolved gasses to cool rapidly leading eventually to crystallisation forming crystals rich in heavy metallic ions surrounded by lighter non-metallic cations.
Such structures resemble closely related arrangements seen elsewhere throughout nature suggesting common origins dating perhaps billions of years earlier still.
Indeed scientists believe our planet itself formed via similar processes involving collisions amongst smaller bodies orbiting nearby stars millions upon trillions kilometres away across interstellar space.
So far no-one else appears aware yet either of exactly how these exotic substances work nor precisely just what role if indeed any might play ultimately determining future fates awaiting humanity beyond mere survival alone…
